column5: mercy and compassion by divine declaration
column6: God proclaims that he will be gracious and compassionate as he chooses; the Hebrew rḥm forms give a direct antecedent for mercy both expansive and particularly bestowed.

column5: poor person's cloak and divine compassion
column6: The law requires returning a poor person's sole covering before night because God hears the cry and is compassionate, joining divine character to practical aid.
David chooses to fall into the Lord's hand during punishment because the Lord's compassions are many, a specific mercy-and-reckoning scene.
Solomon asks God to forgive Israel and grant it compassion before its captors; divine forgiveness is meant to generate merciful treatment in a human relationship.
The Lord is gracious and compassionate to Israel because of covenant and does not yet destroy or cast it away, an enduring mercy within historical judgment.
After the difficult command against an apostate city, God promises mercy, compassion, and multiplication; it is a close case of a hard act framed by later good.
God's compassion is enacted as return and gathering from exile, making mercy a concrete restoration of a scattered family.

column5: pity moved by the oppressed's groaning
column6: The Lord raises saviors and is moved to pity by Israel's groaning under oppressors, a narrative of compassion becoming deliverance.
Israel cries in distress and God gives saviors according to great mercies, pairing a plea for help with prior merciful intervention.
The confession says God's many mercies prevented him from making an end of Israel or forsaking it, directly expressing lasting mercy after rebellion.

column5: return to a gracious and compassionate God
column6: The call to return says God is gracious and compassionate and will not turn his face away, closely joining return, divine face, and mercy.

column5: the just Lord waiting to show compassion
column6: Isaiah names the Lord as a God of justice who waits to be gracious and rises to show compassion, an explicit mercy-and-judgment balance.

column5: made from the womb and helped
column6: The Lord identifies himself as maker and former from the womb, then promises help; this tightly joins prenatal formation with protective care.

column5: former from the womb and sole Creator
column6: The Redeemer who formed Israel from the womb is also the one who alone made all things, directly meeting womb imagery with cosmic creative sovereignty.
After saying Zion was forsaken briefly, God promises to gather her with great compassion, a necessary earlier movement in the mercy sequence continued at 54:10.
The returning wicked person finds God's compassion and abundant pardon, a direct mercy-and-repentance formulation.
God summons faithless Israel to return and says he will not keep anger forever because he is merciful, giving mercy a concrete role in judgment.
God promises never to turn from doing his people good and to preserve their reverence, an unusually explicit account of continuing beneficent care.

column5: rejoicing to do good and plant securely
column6: God's delight in doing his people good and planting them securely turns covenant mercy into settled restoration.

column5: no pleasure in a wicked person's death
column6: God calls the wicked to turn and live rather than die, grounding warning and judgment in a life-seeking divine intention.
Daniel confesses that mercies and forgiveness belong to the Lord even though the people have rebelled, a prayerful mercy-before-pardon formulation.
The person who confesses and leaves sin receives mercy, giving a wisdom-text counterpart to mercy that enables repentance without excusing wrongdoing.
Lamentations says God does not willingly afflict or grieve human beings, sharpening the preceding claim that grief can coexist with compassion.

column5: father sparing a serving son on the day
column6: God promises to spare those who serve him as a man spares a son; mercy, filial imagery, service, and the coming day meet in one verse.
God's return to Jerusalem with mercy entails rebuilding his house there, showing mercy as restoration rather than an inward disposition.
God saves and brings back divided houses because he has compassion, treating them as though he had not rejected them.
God hears enslaved people's groaning and remembers covenant, a concrete sequence of suffering, divine attention, and remembered relation.
God describes seeing, hearing, and knowing Israel's suffering, supplying the emotional and attentive side of merciful rescue.

column5: coming down to deliver and lead
column6: God's response to the preceding cry is descent, liberation, and leading to a land, a full action-pattern for mercy.

column5: one maker forming both in the womb
column6: Job grounds just treatment of servants in the single God who formed master and servant in the womb, joining womb origin to social mercy.
God keeps covenant and loyal love with those who love him through a thousand generations, a durable and relational form of mercy.

column5: not hardening heart against poor kin
column6: The law forbids hardening the heart or closing the hand against a poor brother or sister, explicitly pairing inner hardness with failure of kin-directed mercy.

column5: opening the hand and supplying need
column6: The required alternative is to open the hand freely and lend enough for the need, making mercy an adequate material response.
Generosity must be given without inner resentment, a close ethical counterpart to the commentary's distinction between a gift and a reproached gift.
The Israelite must support a brother who becomes poor so that he can live nearby, a direct scriptural meeting of kinship and sustaining care.

column5: giving to poor as lending to the Lord
column6: Kindness to the poor is treated as a loan to the Lord, connecting help for a weak person to God's own accounting and return.

column5: closing the ear to a poor cry
column6: The person who ignores the poor person's cry will himself cry without answer, a sharp reciprocal warning about refusing mercy.
The opening prophetic call specifies defending the orphan and pleading for the widow, giving concrete content to a softened and just heart.

column5: pouring oneself out for hungry and afflicted
column6: The fast Isaiah commends expends oneself for the hungry and satisfies the afflicted; light then rises out of darkness, connecting mercy to costly action and renewal.
Daniel tells the king to break with sin by righteousness and with iniquity by showing mercy to the oppressed, making mercy a corrective political act.

column5: bread for hungry and clothing for naked
column6: The righteous person gives bread to the hungry and covers the naked, a close prophetic counterpart to mercy measured by what reaches the weak.
Wisdom says God's manner of judging teaches the righteous to be kind and gives hope of repentance, directly linking mercy, justice, and ethical imitation.
Sirach calls the Lord compassionate and merciful, forgiving sins and saving in affliction, a compact wisdom formula for mercy under distress.

column5: mercy and forgiveness for those who return
column6: The text praises the Lord's great mercy and forgiveness toward those who turn to him, extending the return-and-mercy pattern into later Jewish wisdom.

column5: afflicting, showing mercy, and raising from death
column6: Tobit's hymn says God both afflicts and shows mercy, leads down to Hades and brings up again; this strongly parallels mercy, hardship, and resurrection in one confession.

column5: great mercy shown in a birth and shared by kin
column6: Elizabeth's neighbors and relatives hear that the Lord magnified mercy to her and rejoice, joining pregnancy, kinship, and communal recognition of mercy.
The dawn from on high guides feet into the way of peace, the necessary continuation of Luke 1:78's tender-mercy claim and a direct mercy-to-guidance sequence.

column5: kindness to ungrateful and evil people
column6: Jesus grounds enemy-love in the Most High's kindness to the ungrateful and wicked, a particularly demanding account of broad divine mercy.

column5: bandaging and paying for the wounded man
column6: The Samaritan's compassion becomes wounds treated, transport, lodging, and payment, supplying the concrete middle action between feeling compassion and being named merciful.

column5: dead and alive, lost and found
column6: The father's celebration interprets the restored son as dead now alive and lost now found, a mercy scene with resurrection-shaped language.
The tax collector, rather than the self-assured worshiper, goes home justified; this is the necessary outcome of the preceding appeal for mercy in a judgment setting.
The Son of Man's stated mission is to seek and save the lost, a concentrated Christian expression of merciful initiative before the lost can restore themselves.
Jesus is moved with compassion, touches a leper, and heals him; compassion crosses impurity boundaries and becomes bodily restoration.
Jesus sends the healed man home to tell what the Lord has done and how he had mercy on him, linking received aid to grateful witness among kin.
Jesus sees a crowd as sheep without a shepherd, has compassion, and begins to teach them; mercy here supplies instruction as well as care.

column5: compassion that will not send the hungry away
column6: Jesus names his compassion for a crowd without food and refuses to dismiss them hungry, closely matching mercy as feeding the weak.
The Lord sees a widow grieving her only son, has compassion, and addresses her sorrow; the maternal and vulnerable situation makes the link specific.
Jesus compares his desired protection of Jerusalem's children to a bird gathering its brood, a maternal shelter image beside the commentary's protecting womb-home.
The king is moved with compassion, releases the servant, and forgives the debt, supplying the prior mercy that grounds the later command to forgive another.
The parable closes with judgment on those who do not forgive from the heart, keeping received mercy morally serious and accountable.

column5: service to the least received by the King
column6: The king identifies care for hungry, stranger, naked, sick, and imprisoned people as care received by himself, binding mercy to the final royal judgment.

column5: refusing the least as refusal before judgment
column6: The negative verdict treats withholding care from the least as withholding it from the judge, a counter-scene to mercy enacted toward the weak.

column5: poor sibling lacking clothes and food
column6: The verse supplies the concrete needy sibling whose unmet need makes the following empty blessing morally insufficient.
Christ dies for the weak at the right time, a specific Christian claim that saving action meets incapacity rather than prior achievement.

column5: love acting while people are sinners
column6: God demonstrates love in Christ's death while people are still sinners, another explicit formulation of mercy taking the first step.
God's consolation in affliction equips believers to comfort others, extending the Father-of-mercies title into reciprocal human care.
Believers are commanded to be kind and tenderhearted, forgiving as God forgave them; inward tenderness and concrete reconciliation are held together.
The community is to put on compassion with kindness and humility, a direct ethical counterpart to merciful servants walking gently.

column5: nursing mother caring for her children
column6: Paul compares his gentle care for the community to a nursing mother caring for her own children, a close Christian maternal-nurture image.

column5: divine kindness and love for humanity appearing
column6: The appearance of God's kindness and philanthropy is the necessary opening of the mercy-and-rebirth claim in the following verse.
The divine parent disciplines for the believers' good so they may share holiness, clarifying the beneficial end of the hard action named at 12:6.

column5: from not receiving mercy to receiving it
column6: The community's identity is defined by having once lacked mercy and now received it, a direct transformation by bestowed mercy.
The God of all grace restores, confirms, strengthens, and establishes people after they suffer a little while, a sustained-care reading of hardship.
The command to love in deed and truth completes the preceding warning about withholding goods, making action the proof of compassion.
The community is told to have mercy on those who doubt, a direct interpersonal use of mercy toward spiritual weakness.

column5: saving from fire with fearful mercy
column6: Mercy is joined to rescuing some from fire and maintaining fear of corruption, closely holding compassion and grave danger together.

column5: shepherding, living water, and wiped tears
column6: The Lamb shepherds the redeemed, leads them to springs of living water, and God wipes their tears; final sovereignty is rendered as tender provision.
Jesus promises not to leave disciples as orphans but to come to them, a specific parental-care image for mercy that prevents abandonment.

column5: the Word as unique Son from the Father
column6: John claims that the Word became flesh and bears the glory of the unique Son from the Father, a fuller Christian counter-narrative to the commentary's denial of divine child language.

column5: mercy and forgiveness as reciprocal discipline
column6: The early Christian letter exhorts mercy and forgiveness in the measure one hopes to receive them, extending Gospel mercy into a communal rule.

column5: Hagar naming the God who sees her
column6: The pregnant and afflicted Hagar calls God the one who sees her; the connection is a maternal vulnerability answered by divine attention rather than the rḥm vocabulary itself.

column5: water opened to mother and child
column6: God opens Hagar's eyes to a well for her endangered child, a narrative of preemptive provision in a maternal crisis.
The shepherd gives eternal life and says no one will snatch the sheep from his hand, a pastoral image of enduring protective care.

column5: the teacher who instructs and reminds
column6: The Spirit is sent to teach and remind disciples, a Christian teaching-and-guidance scene adjacent to the commentary's Rahmân who teaches.

column5: prayers and alms remembered before God
column6: Cornelius's prayers and alms rise as a memorial before God, linking practical generosity and prayer without making either a purchase of mercy.

column5: doing good to all and to the household of faith
column6: The command combines broad beneficence with a particular household obligation, a modest Christian analogue to wide and kin-directed care.

column5: gifts used to serve one another
column6: Each received gift is to be used in service to others as stewardship of varied grace, a downstream ethic of gifts becoming help.

column5: waiting for mercy into eternal life
column6: Believers keep themselves in God's love while awaiting mercy leading to eternal life, a future-facing mercy frame for the day of fulfillment.

column5: acts of lovingkindness without fixed measure
column6: The Mishnah counts deeds of lovingkindness among practices whose fruit is enjoyed now and whose principal remains for the future, giving mercy an ongoing communal form.
The Didache orders unhesitating giving to those who ask and grounds distribution in the Father's gifts, a later Christian rule for mercy before return.

column5: mercy passing at the judgment seat
column6: In the commonly cited English numbering, 4 Ezra says compassion passes away when the Most High appears for judgment; it is a Jewish apocalyptic counterweight to mercy framing the final day.
